title: First crossings of global warming levels in CMIP6 in light of observed 1.5 °C exceedance
abstract: The year 2024 marked the first time global temperatures exceeded 1.5 °C, raising questions about climate projection accuracy and implications for climate goals. We quantify the timing and likelihood of first crossing 1.5 °C and higher global warming levels across CMIP6 models. The observed 2024 crossing occurred 3–7 years earlier than in CMIP6 projections. Models with high present-day warming rates predicted the timing of the 1.5 °C crossing more accurately, while the 2024 timing is likely affected by internal climate variability superimposed on the anthropogenic trend. A pre-mid-century 2 °C crossing is difficult to avoid even under stringent mitigation (75% of models crossing 2 °C under SSP1-2.6). However, while shifting from high (SSP5-8.5) to medium-high (SSP3-7.0) emissions delays a 3 °C crossing by 10 years, low-emission pathways (SSP1-2.6) avoid crossing this threshold in 85% of models. While near-term 2 °C exceedance is a significant risk, immediate mitigation remains critical to enable adaptation and avoid long-term warming.
problem: The observed 2024 crossing of the 1.5°C warming threshold occurred 3-7 years earlier than projected by CMIP6 climate models, raising questions about their accuracy and the influence of internal climate variability and model-inherent warming rates on future projections.
method: This study systematically quantifies the timing and likelihood of crossing global warming thresholds by analyzing a large ensemble of CMIP6 models, using Kaplan-Meier estimates to calculate exceedance probabilities and comparing the results to observational data.
task: The task is to quantify the timing and likelihood of first crossing various global warming levels using CMIP6 models and to compare these projections to the observed 1.5°C exceedance in 2024.

We utilize three SMILEs from the CMIP6 archive: CanESM5 (25 members), ACCESS-ESM1-5 (40 members) and MIRO6 (50 members). These specific SMILEs were selected to represent a broad spectrum of Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity (ECS), ensuring our assessment of internal variability is contextualized across different model climate sensitivities: MIROC6 has an ECS of 2.6K (which is close to the best IPCC esti- mate of 1.5-4K [37]), ACCESS-ESM1-5 has a mid-range ECS of 3.9K and CanESM5 has a high-end ECS of 5.6K [38].

Here, we address these research gaps by systematically quantifying the timing and likelihood when multiple global warming thresholds-from 1.0°C to 5.0°C-are first crossed using a large ensemble of CMIP6 models. We first compare the observed 2024 crossing of the 1.5°C level against CMIP6 projections across a range of emission pathways (SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5) and evaluate how accurately models projected this observed crossing.
